implementerProof.how: I drove the same surface myself: INFRA-589's committed harness (#2369's packages/envoy/loadtest; Postgres 16.2, 1 ms proxy, NATS, listener). envoy-dispatch was built by the tester from the workspace at 26a15dcf (head) and from lt-before at c892b97d (base). (1) The smoke steps, out-of-order commit: on head, an open psql write held id 10005, the comment POST got 201 in 123 ms as id 10006, and the open stream sent nothing until the commit. Then it sent 10005 and 10006, and a resume sent the same. On base, the stream sent 10006 at once and never 10005. (2) The lock check: with pg_advisory_xact_lock(0x4449535041544348) held, the comment POST on head got 201 in 174 ms. On base it got no answer in 8 s. (3) One 1x load pair on the committed harness. The commit-order lock was held 100% on base and 0% on head. Committed went from 1.90 to 2.48 events/s. Comment p50 went from 26.3 s to 9.3 s. These agree in direction with the implementer's medians (1.18 to 2.88, 28.0 s to 10.7 s). Requests 2xx went from 54% to 45% in my single pair, against 38% to 58% in the implementer's medians. That is a single-run spread, and no acceptance line sets a threshold on it.

proof.criterion: The global serialization is gone: a write holds no lock shared with writes to other issues.
proof.surface: Local Dispatch (envoy-dispatch built from the head's code) on INFRA-589's committed harness, through the REST API, and the harness's 1 s ungranted-lock sampler under the 1x load
proof.command: python3 lockcheck.py (psql holds pg_advisory_xact_lock(0x4449535041544348), and a psql write stays open on LGC-19 with its owner row locked; then POST /api/v1/issues/LGC-190/comments and POST /api/v1/issues/LGC-19/comments); run-step.sh tester-after-1x --events 4 --sessions 400 --requests 60
proof.observed: The POST on LGC-190 got 201 in 174 ms. The POST on LGC-19 waited for the open write on that issue's row, as per-issue order requires. Under 1x load the commit-order lock was held in 0% of samples. The waits sampled were transactionid row_wait on issues rows (select ... from issues where key = $1 for no key update), tuple locks on issues, and the NOTIFY commit lock in 1% of samples (kept by decision D1).
proof.negativeControl: Base c892b97d, same lockcheck: the POST on LGC-190 got no answer within 8 s while the old lock was held. In the base 1x step the commit-order lock was held in 100% of samples, with 45 writers waiting at the median (51 at most).

proof.criterion: A reader resuming from a cursor never misses an event that commits later with a lower id; a test commits two writes out of id order and a resuming reader gets both in a defined order.
proof.surface: GET /api/v1/events (SSE) cold and with Last-Event-ID, on one and on two envoy-dispatch processes sharing one Postgres
proof.command: adv.py rollback commit; adv.py rollback; adv.py concurrent; STREAM_PORT=18778 adv.py concurrent (streams on a second process); adv.py stall; adv.py lastid
proof.observed: Open lower id 10005, committed higher id 10006: the stream sent nothing for 2 s, then 10005 and 10006 in that order, and a resume from 10004 sent the same. When the lower write rolled back, the stream sent 10006 70 ms after the rollback. Concurrency: 80 POSTs ran beside 16 psql writes that each stayed open for 0.2 to 3 s, 4 of which rolled back. Each of 3 cold streams got exactly the 92 committed ids in increasing order, and a resume mid-run got every later id. The run with the streams on the second process gave the same result. A transaction holding a transaction id in another database held the stream back; the event arrived 117 ms after that transaction committed, and the stall warning named the holder. Last-Event-ID 0 replayed all 10,007 rows, equal to the database. An id above the newest still carries a later event. Non-numeric and out-of-range values are refused 400 INVALID_QUERY.
proof.negativeControl: Base c892b97d: the open stream sent 10006 at once and never 10005. In the concurrency run, each of the 3 base streams missed 10 committed ids ([10011, 10012, 10014, 10018, 10021, 10022, 10025, 10028, 10029, 10072]), and so did the mid-run resume.

proof.criterion: Every consumer of the event stream keeps the order it relies on; the plan lists each and the test covers each.
proof.surface: SSE handler and resume, the relay across two processes, GET /api/v1/references?since= on the merged graph query, the outbox's per-issue NATS subject, an event log reset
proof.command: adv.py concurrent (one and two processes); adv.py refs; a raw NATS subscriber on notifications.dispatch.issue.<key>.> during 30 concurrent POSTs on one issue and 30 on ten others; adv.py reset (truncate events restart identity cascade under an open stream)
proof.observed: SSE and relay: as in the criterion above. References: a mention at 10006 stayed out of 3 since=10004 reads while 10005 was open, and appeared once 10005 committed. The Through bound sits on the outer select over every arm, block_refs included (refs/graph.go:241-258). NATS: LGB-28's subject carried seqs 11 to 40, in the order of the database's ids. Reset: after the next commit the relay logged 'the event log was reset' and ended its open streams, and a resume with the old id went on with the new log. The delivery hub has no reachable surface on this stack, since it needs delivery_settings proven against the GitHub App, so it rests on test T6, which CI's Go lanes run.
proof.negativeControl: Base c892b97d, the same references read: the mention at 10102 was listed on every since read while the lower id 10101 was open, uncapped, so a poller moving its since to 10102 would never see a mention at 10101.

risks: Shown on the real surface: on a newly started process, the first SSE connection gets no response headers and no ': open' line while any transaction holds a transaction id anywhere on the Postgres instance. The relay's start waits in Horizon.Await (event_stream_relay.go:190, awaitEventCursor). In the test a transaction in database postgres held it 6 s and more; the base build opened in 49 ms. Every browser reconnect after a deploy waits that long, and the stall warning names the holder. It is the cost the PR already records (live readers wait for open writers), but at connection open rather than per frame.
